questions.question: Can you determine if a QR code leads to a safe website just by examining its black-and-white square pixel pattern?

options.text: Yes, malicious QR codes have irregular distorted corner patterns.
No, all QR codes visually encode binary data and look inert regardless of destination safety.
Yes, if the QR code is printed in high resolution, it is legitimate.
Yes, only authorized organizations can generate dense pixel grids.

questions.explanation: QR codes are simply 2D optical barcodes that encode text or URLs into binary matrix modules. Safe and malicious destinations look identical to human eyesight.
questions.safety_takeaway: Never judge safety by appearance; always preview and verify the root domain.

questions.question: While paying for street parking, you notice a glossy QR sticker pasted directly over the city's metal payment plaque. What should you do?

options.text: Scan the sticker immediately to avoid getting a parking ticket.
Do not scan the sticker; use the meter's physical payment slot or verified city app.
Peel the sticker off halfway to see the original logo, then scan it.
Scan the code, but only browse the page without paying.

questions.explanation: Physical sticker overlay (quishing) is a widespread real-world attack where scammers paste fake stickers over parking meters and charging stations.
questions.safety_takeaway: Feel for tactile sticker edges; avoid scanning unsolicited adhesive overlays.

questions.question: A QR code opens a web page that starts with 'https://' and shows a secure padlock. Does this prove the destination is not a phishing site?

options.text: Yes, the padlock icon guarantees the website has been vetted by security authorities.
No, HTTPS only encrypts data in transit; attackers easily obtain free TLS certificates for phishing domains.
Yes, browsers block unverified certificates automatically.
Yes, phishing websites cannot technically run on HTTPS protocol.

questions.explanation: HTTPS encryption secures communication against eavesdroppers between you and the server. It does not authenticate the operator's moral intentions or verify site legitimacy.
questions.safety_takeaway: HTTPS encrypts transmission; it does not validate domain trustworthiness.

questions.question: What is the recommended security practice when your smartphone camera scans a QR code?

options.text: Configure the camera to automatically open all scanned URLs immediately in the browser.
Read the small URL preview banner and verify the registered domain before tapping to open.
Assume the QR code is safe if it was printed on glossy paper.
Always tap 'Open' first and check the site once it has fully loaded.

questions.explanation: Modern smartphones display a preview banner containing the decoded URL. Inspecting the root domain beforehand prevents accidental visits to drive-by exploit or phishing pages.
questions.safety_takeaway: Always preview the destination link before permitting your browser to launch.

questions.question: Why do QR codes continue to scan successfully even when customized with brand logos or partially damaged?

options.text: QR codes contain built-in Reed-Solomon error correction that reconstructs missing data.
Smartphone cameras query an online database to retrieve missing visual parts.
Attackers disable error correction to execute code on the scanner device.
Logos are interpreted as administrative bypass keys by the scanning software.

questions.explanation: Reed-Solomon error correction allows QR codes to tolerate between 7% and 30% area damage or logo placement while preserving data integrity.
questions.safety_takeaway: A fancy embedded logo does not mean the QR code was officially certified.

questions.question: How does QShield process uploaded QR codes and web addresses safely during inspection?

options.text: It executes all JavaScript scripts in a hidden background sandbox.
It decodes images in-memory and performs static heuristic parsing without rendering or navigating.
It sends automatic login credentials to verify server responses.
It downloads all linked files to test if they contain computer viruses.

questions.explanation: Safe inspection tools decode matrices and evaluate structural string characteristics in memory without making active HTTP requests or executing client code.
questions.safety_takeaway: Static, inert inspection eliminates the risk of drive-by malware execution.

questions.question: You receive an email claiming: 'Your email account will be deleted in 2 hours! Scan this QR code to verify your credentials.' Why is this suspicious?

options.text: Because authentic IT departments only contact employees using postal mail.
Attackers manufacture artificial urgency and use QR codes to bypass email spam filters.
Because accounts cannot be terminated on weekdays.
Because QR codes cannot be delivered inside email attachments.

questions.explanation: Artificial urgency triggers fear and panic, prompting victims to bypass critical thinking. QR codes in emails (quishing) conceal malicious links from traditional text-based scanners.
questions.safety_takeaway: Treat unexpected countdowns and urgency claims as immediate red flags.

questions.question: A QR code on an office printer directs to 'https://login.micros0ft-portal.net/auth'. What threat pattern does this illustrate?

options.text: A standard cloud mirror managed by Microsoft.
Typosquatting/brand mimicry replacing the letter 'o' with a zero to impersonate a trusted portal.
A secure high-performance corporate sub-network.
A valid domain name because it ends in '.net'.

questions.explanation: Typosquatting uses subtle misspellings (such as replacing the letter 'o' with zero '0' or adding extra hyphens) to trick users into submitting credentials on rogue lookalike servers.
questions.safety_takeaway: Scrutinize exact domain spelling before entering login credentials.

questions.question: If a webpage opened via an unfamiliar QR code prompts you to enter your username, password, and instant SMS OTP, what is the risk?

options.text: No risk, because entering an OTP protects you from being phished.
Attackers operate adversary-in-the-middle reverse proxies that harvest OTPs in real-time to hijack accounts.
OTPs cannot be captured over web forms.
The phone carrier automatically blocks fraudulent OTP submissions.

questions.explanation: Modern phishing kits act as live proxies: when you enter an OTP on a fake portal, the attacker's script submits it to the genuine service in real time to compromise your active session.
questions.safety_takeaway: Never enter one-time codes on pages reached through unsolicited QR codes.

questions.question: What should be your immediate first step if you realize you entered your corporate password on a fake QR phishing page?

options.text: Restart your computer and wait 24 hours to see if anything happens.
Change your password immediately on the authentic service, terminate active sessions, and notify IT.
Send an angry email to the phishing website administrator.
Delete your browser history to erase the leaked credentials.

questions.explanation: Time is critical after a credential leak. Immediately changing your password on the genuine site and invalidating active sessions prevents attackers from maintaining access.
questions.safety_takeaway: Act quickly: change compromised passwords and revoke session tokens immediately.

questions.question: A postcard in your mailbox says: 'Package delivery failed! Scan QR to reschedule delivery fee of $1.50.' What is the underlying scam?

options.text: The postal service requires payment updates for all parcel sizes.
A quishing scam designed to harvest credit card numbers, billing addresses, and CVVs.
A standard parcel tracking barcode with no financial component.
An automated system to confirm the recipient's physical signature.

questions.explanation: Small, nominal fee requests ($1.00-$2.00) lower psychological resistance, tempting victims into inputting valuable credit card details that scammers sell or abuse.
questions.safety_takeaway: Verify failed deliveries on the carrier's official website using your tracking number.

questions.question: Why do quishing attackers often impersonate company HR or payroll departments in QR code emails?

options.text: Because HR emails cannot be filtered by enterprise firewall rules.
Employees naturally comply with requests regarding pay raises, benefits, or employee reviews.
Because HR portals require unencrypted connections.
Because mobile phones automatically trust emails sent from human resources.

questions.explanation: Social engineers exploit workplace authority and financial curiosity (e.g. 'Annual Salary Review QR'). Employees scan with mobile devices that bypass corporate desktop defenses.
questions.safety_takeaway: Confirm internal company surveys or policies through official internal channels.

questions.question: You are selling a refrigerator online. A buyer messages: 'I am sending the payment; scan this QR code and enter your UPI PIN to receive ₹15,000.' What will happen if you do this?

options.text: You will successfully receive the ₹15,000 into your bank account.
Your account will be debited ₹15,000 because entering a UPI PIN always authorizes money leaving your account.
The transaction will stay on hold until you confirm your birthdate.
Your bank will require dual authorization from the buyer.

questions.explanation: In UPI architecture, receiving funds is completely passive. You NEVER scan a QR code or enter your secret UPI PIN to receive money. Entering a PIN always authorizes a payment out.
questions.safety_takeaway: Entering your UPI PIN ALWAYS debits your account; receiving money requires no PIN.

questions.question: Before authorizing a UPI transaction at a merchant store, what crucial detail should you verify inside your banking app?

options.text: The battery level of your mobile device.
The verified payee name and Virtual Payment Address (VPA) displayed on your confirmation screen.
The color scheme of the merchant's physical standee.
The number of customers standing in line.

questions.explanation: Scammers sometimes place rogue QR stickers over genuine shop counters. Always ensure the payee name displayed inside your banking app matches the business you are paying.
questions.safety_takeaway: Cross-check the payee name and VPA before confirming any financial payment.

questions.question: Can a malicious payment QR code be generated to automatically set an unauthorized debit amount?

options.text: No, QR codes can only encode contact email addresses.
Yes, UPI URI standards support an optional 'am' (amount) parameter that pre-fills the debit value.
No, banking apps forbid pre-filled amounts in optical codes.
Only government banks can pre-populate transaction amounts.

questions.explanation: The UPI specification (`upi://pay?pa=...&am=5000`) allows pre-specifying payment amounts. Always inspect the amount field before entering your PIN.
questions.safety_takeaway: Verify both the payee name and the exact debit amount before authorizing.

questions.question: You receive a WhatsApp message displaying a ₹2,500 'festival cashback' scratch card with a QR code. What is the safest response?

options.text: Scan the QR code quickly before the reward timer expires.
Delete the message and do not scan; authentic cashbacks are credited directly without scanning QR codes.
Forward the message to 10 friends to verify if it works for them.
Scan the code but enter a wrong PIN to test the system.

questions.explanation: Cashback scratch-card scams are widespread across digital messaging. Legitimate bank rewards deposit money directly into linked accounts without requesting PINs or QR scans.
questions.safety_takeaway: Never scan QR codes sent via social apps to claim prizes or cashbacks.

questions.question: If you inadvertently fell victim to a fraudulent QR payment scam in India, what official emergency action should you take?

options.text: Call the National Cyber Crime Helpline at 1930 and report on cybercrime.gov.in immediately.
Wait for your monthly account statement to dispute the charge.
Post about the scam on social media and wait for a response.
Format your smartphone immediately to delete transaction records.

questions.explanation: Calling 1930 immediately connects victims to the Citizen Financial Cyber Fraud Reporting System, which can freeze stolen funds before fraudsters siphon them from mule accounts.
questions.safety_takeaway: Act within the golden hour: report financial fraud immediately to 1930.

questions.question: A caller posing as customer support says: 'Your failed delivery refund is ready; scan this QR code on WhatsApp to collect your money.' What should you do?

options.text: Scan the QR code and approve the request to claim your refund.
Refuse the request; legitimate company refunds are processed automatically back to the original source.
Ask them to send the QR code by SMS instead.
Share your credit card number over the phone instead.

questions.explanation: Customer support agents never send QR codes to refund money. Automated refunds return to the original payment instrument without requiring user-initiated QR transfers.
questions.safety_takeaway: Refunds never require you to scan a barcode or approve a collection request.

questions.question: In the web address 'https://chase.com.security-verify.xyz/login', what is the actual registered domain you will connect to?

options.text: chase.com, because it is at the front of the host string.
security-verify.xyz, because the registered domain sits immediately before the top-level domain.
login, because it is the terminal file path.
Both chase.com and security-verify.xyz equally.

questions.explanation: Domain names are evaluated hierarchically from right to left. 'chase.com' in this address is merely an unauthorized subdomain prefix created on the rogue domain 'security-verify.xyz'.
questions.safety_takeaway: Identify the real root domain before the suffix; prefixes are easily spoofed.

questions.question: A QR code directs your browser to 'http://198.51.100.45/account/update'. Why does QShield flag raw IP hosts with high risk?

options.text: Because raw IP addresses cannot transmit HTML code.
Legitimate consumer websites use registered domain names; raw IPs are commonly used by short-lived phishing servers.
Because mobile phone browsers cannot connect to IP addresses.
Because IP addresses indicate an encrypted VPN tunnel.

questions.explanation: Legitimate brands invest in verified domain names and SSL infrastructure. Using a raw IP address in consumer-facing communications is a common indicator of transient malicious hosting.
questions.safety_takeaway: Exercise extreme caution when links use raw IP numbers instead of recognizable domain names.

questions.question: Why should users exercise elevated caution when scanning a QR code that encodes a shortened link (e.g. bit.ly, tinyurl)?

options.text: Shortened links are illegal under international telecommunication rules.
Shorteners completely conceal the actual destination URL from preview inspection.
Shorteners automatically download smartphone applications without consent.
Shortened links cannot be decoded by modern smartphone cameras.

questions.explanation: URL shorteners conceal the true endpoint, making it impossible to evaluate destination safety by visual inspection alone. Safe redirect inspectors help preview final targets.
questions.safety_takeaway: Use safe redirect preview tools before following shortened links from unknown sources.

questions.question: What is an Internationalized Domain Name (IDN) homoglyph attack?

options.text: Using foreign characters (e.g. Cyrillic 'а') that look identical to Latin letters to mislead users into fake domains.
Translating website text automatically into foreign languages without permission.
Cracking Wi-Fi router passwords using dictionary wordlists.
Sending duplicate QR codes to multiple mobile devices simultaneously.

questions.explanation: Homoglyph attacks exploit lookalike glyphs across different alphabets (e.g. Cyrillic 'а' vs Latin 'a'). In standard ASCII, these domains appear prefixed with 'xn--' (punycode).
questions.safety_takeaway: Watch out for punycode ('xn--') domains that visually mimic familiar brands.

questions.question: A QR code decodes to 'https://portal.bank-update.com:8443/login'. What does the ':8443' portion represent?

options.text: The year the web server certificate was created.
A non-standard network port specification instead of standard HTTPS port 443.
A verified customer service phone extension.
The encrypted security level of the webpage.

questions.explanation: Standard web traffic utilizes port 80 (HTTP) or 443 (HTTPS). Non-standard ports (like 8080 or 8443) may point to administrative interfaces, staging environments, or rogue proxies.
questions.safety_takeaway: Non-standard port numbers on consumer login pages warrant additional scrutiny.

questions.question: In the link 'https://google.com@attacker-site.org/search', which server will your browser actually contact?

options.text: google.com, because it comes first.
attacker-site.org, because text prior to the '@' symbol is treated as user authentication credentials.
Both servers simultaneously through a split connection.
Neither; browsers refuse to load any address containing an '@' symbol.

questions.explanation: RFC URL standards interpret string elements before '@' as userinfo (`user:pass@host`). Fraudsters abuse this to display a trusted name in front of their rogue server.
questions.safety_takeaway: Text preceding the '@' character in a URL does not represent the destination server.

questions.question: What information does a standard Wi-Fi QR code (`WIFI:S:Cafe_Net;T:WPA;P:secret123;;`) contain?

options.text: Only a link to download the cafe's mobile app.
The plaintext network SSID name, encryption type, and network password.
An encrypted token that only telecom companies can decrypt.
The device MAC address of everyone connected to the network.

questions.explanation: Wi-Fi QR codes embed the wireless network name and access key in readable format. Scanning automatically configures and connects the device without manual password typing.
questions.safety_takeaway: Do not display private home or office Wi-Fi QR codes in publicly viewable areas.

questions.question: What is an 'Evil Twin' Wi-Fi attack in public venues like airports and coffee shops?

options.text: Connecting two smartphones together with a USB cable.
A rogue access point set up by an attacker using the exact same name as the legitimate venue to intercept traffic.
A computer monitor that mirrors your phone screen without Bluetooth.
A software bug that duplicates your contact list.

questions.explanation: Attackers deploy fake hotspots with identical names to trick devices into connecting. Once connected, attackers can intercept unencrypted traffic or stage captive portal phishing.
questions.safety_takeaway: Confirm authentic public Wi-Fi credentials with venue staff before connecting.

questions.question: Why does QShield automatically mask Wi-Fi passwords as '••••••••' when decoding Wi-Fi QR payloads?

options.text: Because QShield cannot decode WPA encryption keys.
To prevent shoulder surfing and stop sensitive network credentials from leaking into screen recordings or logs.
Because the Wi-Fi password has expired.
To force users to purchase a premium subscription.

questions.explanation: Privacy-by-design requires masking sensitive credentials to protect users against accidental disclosure during demonstrations, screen sharing, or diagnostic logs.
questions.safety_takeaway: Responsible security tools protect sensitive credentials from inadvertent exposure.

questions.question: A QR code decodes to 'https://service.example.org/reset?token=xyz987654&email=user@test.org'. What privacy hazard does this present?

options.text: The URL embeds active session tokens and personal emails directly in query parameters.
The URL will automatically deactivate the user's smartphone SIM card.
Web browsers reject any query string longer than ten characters.
There is no hazard because query parameters are always deleted upon scanning.

questions.explanation: Query parameters containing tokens, passwords, or emails can be captured in web server access logs, browser history, and third-party analytics trackers.
questions.safety_takeaway: Never share or publicly inspect QR codes containing active reset tokens or personal credentials.

questions.question: Upon connecting to a public Wi-Fi network, a browser pop-up demands: 'Log in with your Facebook or Google password to access free internet.' Is this safe?

options.text: Yes, standard social login is universally required for airport Wi-Fi.
No, rogue access points use fake captive portals to steal social media and email credentials.
Yes, if the social media logo looks authentic.
Yes, because captive portals run in an isolated operating system sandbox.

questions.explanation: Rogue hotspot operators set up counterfeit captive portals designed to harvest passwords. Authentic public networks typically require email registration or SMS OTP, not your private social media password.
questions.safety_takeaway: Never enter passwords for your primary accounts on Wi-Fi captive login pages.

questions.question: Why does QShield process uploaded QR images in-memory and discard image bytes after matrix decoding?

options.text: To minimize disk wear and ensure user data and photos are never retained on the server.
Because the server has disabled all hard drive storage permissions.
To prevent other website visitors from downloading your photos.
Because OpenCV cannot write files to modern operating systems.

questions.explanation: In-memory processing ensures that user-uploaded documents and QR codes are not permanently persisted on server storage, strictly upholding privacy-by-design standards.
questions.safety_takeaway: Privacy-by-design ensures user data is discarded immediately after analysis.

questions.question: How can a cyber attacker use HTTP redirects (301/302) to evade initial link analysis?

options.text: By redirecting through a benign reputation domain before forwarding victims to an unindexed phishing destination.
By changing the user's browser language automatically.
By encrypting the user's hard drive during the redirect hop.
Redirects cannot be used to evade security scanners.

questions.explanation: Attackers frequently create multi-hop redirect chains where the initial shortener or tracking domain appears clean, but subsequently bounces visitors to an evasive phishing host.
questions.safety_takeaway: Inspect the entire redirect chain to uncover the final true destination.

questions.question: Why does QShield strictly block redirect inspection for IP ranges such as 127.0.0.1, 10.0.0.0/8, and 169.254.169.254?

options.text: Because those IP ranges have been decommissioned by the internet registry.
To prevent Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) attacks targeting local systems and cloud metadata services.
Because internal networks only operate using Bluetooth.
To comply with international copyright streaming guidelines.

questions.explanation: Allowing an online server to make outbound network requests to internal or loopback IP ranges creates high-severity SSRF vulnerabilities that could expose sensitive infrastructure.
questions.safety_takeaway: Safe inspection tools enforce strict network boundaries against private resources.

questions.question: If an external threat intelligence lookup (such as Google Safe Browsing) reports 'No threats detected', does that guarantee a link is safe?

options.text: Yes, reputation feeds detect 100% of phishing links within seconds of creation.
No, newly created phishing domains (zero-day attacks) often remain unlisted for several hours or days.
Yes, if the provider has an enterprise cybersecurity license.
Yes, reputation feeds guarantee financial reimbursement if a site turns out to be fake.

questions.explanation: Threat intelligence databases depend on telemetry and user reports. Brand-new phishing domains operate in the gap before security feeds discover and index them.
questions.safety_takeaway: Reputation checks are valuable, but a clean report never guarantees zero risk.

questions.question: If QShield blocks redirect inspection on a URL because it points to an unresolvable hostname or internal address, does that mean the link is safe to open on your phone?

options.text: Yes, if an inspection tool blocks a connection, it means your personal phone is protected.
No, a blocked or incomplete inspection is a defensive precaution and not an endorsement of safety.
Yes, unresolvable addresses can never cause security issues.
Yes, because the scanning server took the risk on your behalf.

questions.explanation: Inspection boundaries prevent security tools from making unsafe connections. If a link cannot be safely traced, users should treat it with heightened caution, not assume it is benign.
questions.safety_takeaway: Incomplete or blocked inspection is a safety stop, not proof of site safety.

questions.question: What is the safest way to access your bank or airline account if a printed QR code prompts you to make an urgent booking change?

options.text: Scan the printed QR code and accept all browser security warnings.
Open a trusted browser window and manually type the official website address or use the company's verified app.
Search for the company on social media and click the first sponsored link.
Ask someone nearby to scan the code first on their phone.

questions.explanation: Out-of-band verification is the gold standard of quishing defense: bypass the untrusted physical medium entirely and access the verified service directly through official bookmarks or apps.
questions.safety_takeaway: When in doubt, bypass the QR code and navigate directly via trusted official channels.

questions.question: Why does QShield emphasize that its risk score is an explainable heuristic assessment rather than a guarantee?

options.text: Because cybersecurity defense is probabilistic; static structural checks assess risk patterns, not intent.
Because QShield does not have access to computer hardware.
Because all internet security rules expire after thirty days.
Because heuristic scanners are only designed for academic testing.

questions.explanation: Defensive cybersecurity relies on identifying risky structural traits (e.g. typosquatting, raw IPs). Transparent heuristic tools inform user judgment rather than claiming absolute omniscient certainty.
questions.safety_takeaway: Heuristic scores empower user awareness; critical thinking remains your strongest shield.
